utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, The Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Before we start with the direct examination of this witness, there's two matters I would like to announce. All those things are related to the scheduling arrangement. The first thing is that today and tomorrow, in the morning session, we'll finish at 1.30 instead of 1.45, and we'll continue at 3.00 until 4.30. Another matter is on Wednesday, if we have to sit, we have to sit in the afternoon from 2.15 until 7.00. And at the same time, I want to reiterate the Bench's position that if Mr. Blagojevic wants to ask some questions to the witness, the best way is for him to write down his questions on a piece of paper and pass it to his counsel. The statement by the accused normally is not a good way because we sense there's a danger for himself to incriminalise himself. Having said that, could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How are you this morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm well. Thank you. And ready to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd like to start off with a document that has been previously marked as D22/1. You have the original B/C/S version in front of you, if you could just take a moment to look at that. And the English is on the ELMO. You've had a chance to view this document prior to coming to Court today, haven't you, Mr. Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, I have. It is on one of the CDs that the OTP supplied me with, at least my lawyer and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall this document coming to the Zvornik Brigade during the war period?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The kind of document that I'm reading through here and now, coming from the main staff, never arrived. But another one did, a similar one. I would say a copy compiled by the Drina Corps and forwarded to the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know roughly when the Drina Corps' version of this got to the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it as being the winter of 1994, which means probably a little later than the date it states here. The 24th of October is what it says here. So I'm guessing it might have been some 20 days later or thereabouts. I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did this document cause any concern within the command for any reason?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say it did with Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic, the commander. Perhaps the term you used "concern," I don't know whether that's the best term. But yes, in a sense he was rather angry or something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you explain why you think he was angry, what he indicated.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Mr. McCloskey. I saw it as Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic considered that a similar instruction had already been issued, or rather that he had been -- Drago Nikolic, security officer, had been given greater authorisations than he had expected with respect to what Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic thought that security officers should have, should be given.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did Drago Nikolic try to use this document in any way to do anything, increase his authority or his powers?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I ought to say that before this document arrived, not this document but the similar one, the Zvornik Brigade headquarters, that Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic had already ordered that Drago Nikolic was not allowed to send out any mail without his knowledge, and the commander insisted that all his letters be opened from the superior command and from the security organs as well. He also requested that the brigade stamp should not be placed on a signature by Drago Nikolic, and he also asked that Drago Nikolic should do duty work as a duty officer, like everybody else at the forward command post or the command post, wherever. And we'd discussed this previously. So if I remember correctly, in this instruction, certain things were ordered in such a way that Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic had to give up his own concepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did this document allow Drago Nikolic to get out of his obligations to be duty officer at the forward command post or the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in a way --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't get your answer, so let me just ask the question again. Was Drago Nikolic able to get out of the duty officer obligations?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drago Nikolic insisted that he shouldn't be a duty officer, and he attempted to have that prevail. But the commander remained persistent and did not want to give up his ideas so that nonetheless, despite everything, Drago Nikolic was the duty officer both at headquarters and the forward command post when his shift came up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What about communications, as you've talked about? Did this document or the document related to it change the way communications were delivered back and forth to the corps regarding who could look into them and who couldn't?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that after this instruction was given, Drago Nikolic looked at his postal mail, if I can put it that way, the mail he sent out to the security organ of the superior command. That means Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic. He could send that without it having being signed by Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic, so it could be directly signed by Drago Nikolic. And vice versa, the correspondence or communications coming in. If Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic would be sending something and if it was addressed to Second-Lieutenant Drago Nikolic, security organ of the Zvornik Brigade, in person, then those communications would go directly to Drago Nikolic and not to Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to the next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, would you please repeat the number of this document. It seems to me that we missed in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's D22/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next document, it's P117C is the English and D is the B/C/S. And if we could have the B/C/S for the witness and the English for the ELMO. B/C/S is handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, if you could take a little time to review this. I know you've had a chance to review some of these prior to court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra, your objection is still running.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a 12 July intercept at 16.40 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, do you recall this particular conversation?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall it, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall actually having this conversation on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so in your review of this transcript, does this appear to be an accurate transcription of that conversation as far as you can remember way back then?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And already the first sentence says what I told you about two or three days ago, that I sent my intelligence man. I said I sent Captain Vukotic to -- or rather, the 4th Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade, and that's how this begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you -- I won't have you go over that story again, but we may have bits and pieces of it. Who were you speaking to? We see "Obrenovic" and then it says "X." Who is X, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: X was Colonel Jocic from the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know what Jocic's position was that day?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps that day he was the operations duty officer in the Drina Corps. I'm not quite sure. But by establishment, he was in the operations of the -- we called him an operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just want to start. Like you've said in the beginning, you received information from your intelligence officer, and you start providing the corps with, as you say, a detailed picture in the third line. But this -- the fifth line: "The Turks are, my guys had captured a Turk alive, but unfortunately later on they..." And then in parentheses someone in background on Obrenovic side says "that has been shot." And then Jocic says "they have sent him." And you say: "Yes, they have sent him for exchange." Can you explain what that business about -- did someone on your side say that he'd been shot?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that this is Captain Vukotic, that he said that. The communication line was open. It was an open line, the one I used. And he was in the office, and he added this expression as an aside. And it meant that that person had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when you said "yes, they have sent him for exchange," was that true?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As you can see in the previous sentence, I started talking, and I said: "But unfortunately, later on they..." And then Captain Vukotic came in with the comment "that has been shot." And then Colonel Jocic said "they sent him." And then this prompted me to say "yes, they sent him for exchange." Because of the communication line, we knew they were being listened in to, tapped into.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then it says: "They have information from both him and from the spot." So is it your understanding that -- what do you think that means, "they have received information from him"? Which person is the "him"?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, Captain Vukotic was in the 4th Battalion, or rather was 8th Battalion previously. And early in the morning we received information that there was somebody who had been captured up there. But not only because of that, but also because of gaining an insight into the situation, I made the decision and sent Captain Vukotic to this 4th Battalion for the simple reason of gaining an impression as to what we could expect from those forces, along the usual corridors in our direction. So that was the idea, that there was a live prisoner up there somewhere, and Captain Vukotic left. However, while he was on his way to the 4th Battalion, that particular prisoner was no longer alive. And the people he talked to up there told him that -- he received information about the interrogation of that prisoner while he was still alive. And on the spot, the other soldiers told him what had actually happened so that this observation relates to that, that means they have information about the interrogation of that prisoner and also what other soldiers and officers told him in Kajici about the situation there. And it was all to do with the forces that might be moving and advancing towards the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did Vukotic tell you the circumstances surrounding the shooting of this prisoner?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't give me the details. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then the remaining part of this intercept is -- indicates the knowledge you learned about the various forces as you testified to last week. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I had information from Captain Vukotic, but I said that Lieutenant-Colonel Mane Djuric the deputy officer of security in Zvornik called me up who was up there, at Konjevic Polje on the spot or thereabouts, and provided detailed information as to who was where. So Captain Vukotic and Lieutenant-Colonel Mane Djuric were my sources of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On the second page of the English, there's a -- I'm not sure where it is on yours, but there's a mention of -- you say the second group from the Protection Regiment, and then Jocic says "yes," and you say, "patrols along the Kasaba/Jelah axis." Now, who-- again, can you just remind us, who the protection regiment is. Just take a minute if you need to find it.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, it's a battalion of the military police from the 63rd Protection Regiment of the main staff. That's who that is about. And it was permanently located --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just for the record, did you say 63rd or 65th?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I meant the 65th Protection Regiment of the main staff. It's a battalion of theirs that was constantly deployed there and its basic location was in Kasaba. And they were moving along that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And so could you -- can you show us where you learned that they were stationed, if you could use the pointer again, where the Protection Regiment so we know where the Kasaba/Jelah axis is as you state in the intercept?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is where Kasaba is here. And I think that Jelah is -- this is a large-scale map. This is the bridge at Kaldrmica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for the record, that's just south of Nova Kasaba on the map, the bridge at Kaldrmica?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's on the road towards Cerska, that particular bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then that would be north of Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. I apologise. Quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if we could go to the next exhibit, which is P118A, and page 6 for the ELMO. I think it has been marked for you. And the B/C/S has been marked. If you could go to 13 July in that B/C/S exhibit. But first, could you tell us the title of this exhibit, this book that we've given you.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, on the cover here it says "IKM," which means forward command post, Kitovnice. It is the logbook or diary of the duty officer so that we don't get confused, this is the diary or logbook of the duty officer at the forward command post, not the operations duty officer at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters, but the logbook kept by the senior officer at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this is a collection of pages from that notebook that they kept up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you could look to the 13 July entry, it says: "I took over duty (unscheduled) from Lieutenant Drago Nikolic at 2300 hours." And under that is the name "Major Galic." Does this fit into the account that you had provided us earlier, about Drago Nikolic contacting you and asking to be relieved from the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that that was the continuation. When he asked me to relieve him at the forward command post, I said, "See who the next duty officer is according to the schedule." And when that comes about, you call him. So quite obviously, the shift was at 2300 hours which would make it part of that schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would like to object to this -- not to the authenticity -- to the authenticity, but not to the ability of Mr. McCloskey to direct from this document, but I do want to object that up until this morning, this document was missing pages that had to do with July 13th, 14th, and 15th. 13th and 14th. We were just handed these additional pages before Court began today. But up until this time, those pages, 11th, 12th, 13th, and 14th, were missing. And I just, for clarification purposes, need to know whether this was a document provided by Mr. Obrenovic or how they secured this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This document has never had any missing pages. The -- what we provided you were the English translations of one of these newer logbooks that were provided to us, and we have just provided the English translations of those pages. So those things don't have anything to do with this logbook. We'll get to that logbook in a minute. But it's a different logbook as the witness was trying to make that clear. This logbook was obtained in a search warrant of the Zvornik Brigade years ago and has been provided in English and in B/C/S for years now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I will accept the fact that this is not an Obrenovic document. But I do have to object because we were just handed today, this morning, the 13th and 14th out of this logbook which was not part of the documents translated and given to us prior to this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you sure of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm comparing it right now to the one that's on the monitor, and it's exactly the document that we were handed this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart in giving copies of these documents, I don't know a week or so ago, so that everyone knew which exhibits we were using. Last night, we found out that we inadvertently left out the English translation in that handing out, but of course that handing out was only, you know, the most recent version. I mean, recent handing out of the document, this English thing had been around for years. We just missed it when we handed it out at first, so there's nothing new here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As for the documents, this Bench is also worried about the validity of the documents in this case. I believe that in the future, the both parties need not to furnish us with the whole set of the documents again so long as we already have these documents. They could only give us the relevant part of certain documents with the correct indication of from which document those parts come from so that we could find out those documents in our binders back in the office before the sittings. I think this is the most economical way for that. And as for the B/C/S versions, well, I believe that this Bench only needs one copy of the B/C/S version. There's no need for the parties to furnish us with three sets of the B/C/S version because we don't read the B/C/S; we merely rely on the English, and that would reduce a great amount of the work in copying these documents. Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I just want to renew my objection because we just received -- although P18 was provided to us, as the Court has just stated, the most relevant part of P18 had been missing up until this morning. So our objection is that we are surprised by the most relevant part of the document that was just provided this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think we will bear in mind your objections. We will check into our files whether we have those documents furnished to us before. And when we come to the admission of the documents, we'll deal with this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to clarify, this particular document and the import of it was clearly mentioned by Rick Butler and cited by Rick Butler in his report, and the English was provided years ago. So this is not an issue where something new has occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll check it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, at some point after the war were you able to assemble some relevant documents related to the wartime period surrounding Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us about that, when you were able to identify these documents, how you ended up getting them.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, sometime in the early spring of 1999, that is, before the bombing of Yugoslavia, I received a phone call one day from the corps commander who ordered me to go to the Mali Zvornik barracks in the afternoon of that day. He said --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you ID who the corps commander was at that time?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. It was Major-General Svetozar Andric. He said that in the barracks, I would find a man. He didn't mention his name. And he said when I saw him, it would be clear to me, and that I should take measures to provide him with working conditions, accommodation, food, and so on. On that day, I really went there in the Mali Zvornik barracks --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us where Mali Zvornik is.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mali Zvornik is right across the Drina, on the right bank of the River Drina facing Veliki Zvornik, right here. So it's in the Republic of Serbia. At that time, it was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In the barracks I mentioned, I found General Miletic with two other men. I didn't know the other two men, and I still don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was General Miletic the general you mentioned earlier in your testimony, the same one?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The general who was in the main staff during the war, and we mentioned him two or three days ago. I don't remember when exactly. In that room, there was a big pile of documents, and there was a smaller room next to it where they were sitting. This was full of documents. They had a photocopying machine. They were going through the documents, and they copied some of them. This was the first time I saw that pile of documents. Maybe it's not the best way to describe it. But there, I talked to General Miletic. We had coffee. We discussed his accommodation and the other things that General Andric had ordered me to take care of. That was the first time I saw those documents in that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so what did you do?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: One or two days later, or rather on that same day, I had a short conversation with General Miletic. We had coffee and sat down together. But I didn't have an opportunity to look at any of the documents at that point in time. A few days later, one or two days perhaps, I went to the same place in the afternoon to visit the general and to see if everything was all right, to see if everything was as our commander General Andric had ordered. And then I had a longer conversation with General Miletic, but again, I didn't look at the documents or anything else. They completed their review of these documents in five or six days, as I remember now, roughly. After that, to be quite honest, I felt suspicion arise in my mind. I knew that I had been in Zvornik, and that sooner or later the Prosecution would raise the issue of my responsibility in all these matters. And I found it strange that they were looking through these documents, bypassing regular procedure. This was sort of semi-illegal. I don't know if that's the best expression. But then it struck me that it might be a good idea for me to look at these documents as well and to see what there was there. I didn't succeed in this, however, because the soldiers who were there in the barracks, although some of them knew me, told me this was not possible without written permission from General Andric, the corps commander. I called him up, and he told me on the phone to type out a request for this activity, which I did. The courier took it to him, and he gave me written permission saying that I could look through these documents. I received two identical documents without a date, and also the key to that room. On two occasions, one day and the next, I went there and looked through as many documents as I was able to in that time. And on that occasion, I took some of the documents, and those were the ones I handed to you. I copied General Andric's notes of permission in order to be able to enter the room more times, but the guards were there, and the noncommissioned officer who was there would only accept original documents. So I was able to enter the room on only two occasions, and that was the time I had available to look through a portion of the documents. And I took the ones that I gave you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were the documents that you took and provided to us mostly original documents?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The documents I took from Mali Zvornik were originals, and I handed to you several other documents as well which were not from Mali Zvornik, but from the ministry of defence, and those were copies concerning the buses and I don't remember what else. But all the documents from Mali Zvornik are originals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have a photocopying machine there. They took it away before my arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And those documents were provided to the Prosecution pursuant to your guilty plea and plea agreement?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to P119A, and if you could take a look at the photocopy of this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Before Mr. McCloskey goes into this document, P119, this is the document provided by Mr. Obrenovic, and I believe that the chain of custody that Mr. McCloskey has described is an incomplete chain of custody, and we object to these documents as being unreliable at this point because this is -- the chain of custody has been tarnished. And I would like, if Mr. McCloskey is going to try any of the evidence provided by Mr. Obrenovic, that he give a complete chain of custody of these documents prior to going through them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that the chain of custody is very clear from the explanations by this witness and by Mr. McCloskey. Is there something missing, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There is some more detail, Mr. President. My plan was to in private session briefly go through it at the end. I can go through it at this point in private session if you wish. I just was, out of trying to be as efficiency as possible, save that part to the end. But if you prefer, I could do it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Which do you prefer, Ms. Sinatra?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I would ask him to prove that the chain of custody is reliable prior going into any of the Obrenovic documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that was my -- the evidence for chain of custody. There are other witnesses that could be brought in, but it's not the intention of the Prosecution at this time to go any further unless there's any request or need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think you have to wait until you hear the cross-examination of Ms. Sinatra on this issue. Then you decide. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could -- you've had a chance to look at P119. This appears to be a regular combat report from the command of the Drina Corps to the main staff. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is this one of several original Drina Corps daily combat reports that you provided the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recognise the signature at the end of this report?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks to me like the signature of General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If this is, in fact, the signature of General Krstic, could you give us your opinion on who was commander at the time that this document was signed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll object to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would object to that. I think there's a lack of foundation. He's asking the gentleman to speculate based on this one document and this one signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe the question is not a proper one. And could we go through the document first. Then we'll come to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, Mr. President. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe in paragraph -- well, can you just briefly outline what this document does and what it says in relationship to the Zvornik Brigade and the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, this document was issued by the command of the Drina Corps on the 13th of July, 1995. And the document itself is a regular combat report which this command sent to the main staff of Republika Srpska on the same day. And roughly the document contains the following elements: Information about the enemy; under two, the combat readiness of the units of the Drina Corps; three, the situation on the ground in the area of responsibility of the corps; five, security and morale situation, all this referring to the Drina Corps; six, the logistics support. Then the casualties for the previous day and up to the time when the report was sent. And then the conclusion and the order for what is to be done. And finally the signature and the square seal with the code of the telegraph station saying that the document was received on the 13th of July at 19.45. And that the coded document was sent on the same day, the 13th of July at 20.10 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in the decision, what does it have? Does it make any statement about Drina Corps forces?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you allow me to read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Decision with the main forces of the corps: Persistently defend the line with 20-hour reconnaissance and observation of the enemy without interruption so as to avoid any surprises with part of the forces in cooperation of the forces of the MUP; control the depth of the territory; discover, block, imprison, and disarm the forces of the Muslims which have been broken up; the population and material goods, also protecting ourselves from any attack from behind" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there. Were there any Zvornik Brigade troops actually doing this, what the general is saying in this report?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And as you have described earlier, many of things you've described is what is being described in this report?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a summary reflecting precisely this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know from the corps level what the corps generally refers to when they're writing their daily combat report to the main staff?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, there were elements that were prescribed for reporting and which command would report what. Obviously, the Drina command corps had to report on these eight elements I have just read out. Each of these elements was to be reported on with a summary of what had happened on the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But the Zvornik Brigade, for example, what source documents from the Zvornik Brigade, if any, would the Drina Corps use in drafting their daily combat report about what was going on in the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, what they would use, the corps command would use for the elaboration of this document, a regular combat report similar to this one. It would be sent from the command of the Zvornik Brigade one hour prior to that. It would use the extraordinary combat report if that existed depending on the situation. And also, oral reporting from the duty officer which were to be sent out every three to four hours at the time. So they would compile all this information, process it from all the units, and this would be the product of all that. I don't know if I've made myself clear, not only from the Zvornik Brigade but the Bratunac and all the other units, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And in the -- the signature block at the bottom, it says: "Commander, Major-General Radislav Krstic" and it's signed. What was Major-General Krstic the commander of at this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object. I am going to object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think he's -- well, I guess Mr. McCloskey is trying to get through the back door rather than through the front. I think he could ask the gentleman who was the commander at that time because I believe that that was somewhat of a contentious issue during the Krstic case because it would appear that both on the 13th, you have two commanders. The question is who was really in command, who is officially or de facto, de jure, in command, and I think that this gentleman may not be the best possible person to give us a definitive answer. So if he would rephrase, I think he can get to where he wants to go. But the way it's stating it, I believe he's asking the witness to assume certain facts which at least at this point are not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, just ask the witness who was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who was the commander at this time?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, if I read through this document, and it is the report of the 13th of July, 1995, as the commander here, we have the signatory as Major-General Radislav Krstic. Three or four days ago, I said that as to the shift of commanders, I learned from Lieutenant-Colonel Borovcanin at the meeting in my own office on the 15th. So that's what I know about. I can't tell you about the exact hour. I have no precise data about that. If I did, I would tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this document provide any indication of whether or not General Krstic was a commander at the time and date that this document was executed?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this document, the corps commander is General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to the next document, P120A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you could just take a moment to look at that, and can you tell us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, what I'm holding in my hands is an interim report by the command of the 1st Zvornik Brigade for the 14th of July, 1995. Major Dragan Obrenovic is the signatory, me, and the document was compiled by Major Dragan Jokic, and it was typed out by Staff Sergeant Misko Vasic. The document was sent out on the 15th of July, 1995, at 01.10 hours to the superior command. Otherwise, as far as the contents of the document itself goes, it is the following: "Tonight at around 20.20 hours, a large group of Muslims passed through the broader Maricici area, proceeding towards the Zvornik-Caparde Road."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this have to do with anything that you testified about last week?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. I already said at the time that on the evening of the 14th, once we were broken up at Snagavo in the ambush, and when I managed to collect the units up and organise our defence and see what we needed -- see how many casualties we had, I wrote down on a piece of paper precisely this and gave it to the signalsman who relayed it on. And I said that the time I wrote this was most probably around 23 to 2400 hours. And you can see that the document was sent out on the 15th of July at 01.10 hours. So while this was relayed to the radio centre, radio communications centre, and from there to the operations hall, and while these two men typed this out, the time that took, it was conveyed at precisely 01.10 hours, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do you know from this document -- is there any indication from this document that Dragan Jokic was involved as you have said in communicating this document on to the corps?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, this is a poor copy. But in the lower left-hand corner, above the word "chief of staff," there is an abbreviation. In Cyrillic, it says DJ/MV. So according to the rules at the time, this meant the initials of the individual who compiled document and the individual typing out the document. Those are the initials at the bottom, DJ/MV. Here you have the -- here you have it, DJ, the person typing out the document was Dragan Jokic -- no, I'm sorry. The person who compiled the document was Dragan Jokic, and the person doing the typing was MV, Misko Vasic. I don't know whether that was his proper name. But we called him Misko Vasic, and he was from our office there and was a staff sergeant. So this is according to the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could now go to Exhibit P121A, which is a copy of portions of intercepts. And if we could put page 7 in the English on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you could find the 14 July section, Mr. Obrenovic. And I am going to ask if you can find any reference to the radio transmission you spoke about last week relating to engineering officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I just wanted to renew our objections regarding the intercept information. This is a logbook that has not been introduced by the Prosecution, and the reliability and authenticity of the logbook of the intercept operator is, of course, also objected to by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you found any reference to those engineering officers you had mentioned?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. On page 3, the first half of the page there, it says: "For Maric, Miladnovic, and Mitrovic" and then in brackets, it says: "Engineers to come to Nedo's inn with the excavator in order to widen the road." Then it says: "They went to Sava 66."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does that sound familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already spoken about that. Yes, it does sound familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that the information your signalsman gave to you that you spoke of last week?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What is the reference to "Nedo's inn?"

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think that refers to a facility in Orahovac, a coffee shop along the road from Zvornik to Crni Vrh in Orahovac, and I think that was used as a point for them to know where they were supposed to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And if we could go to P123A. This is an intercept dated 14 July at 9.10 in the morning between Milenko Zivanovic and Major Jokic. And if you could briefly review that and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm sorry. This doesn't have to do with the authenticity. This has to do with the fact that we're objecting because Mr. Obrenovic is being requested to give an opinion about a document that he was not a participant in. It is purely speculation on his part as to what these people are signifying. He was not present, and he did not hear this conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we haven't come to this document yet, and it's difficult for me to make a decision at this moment. Shall we go to see how far the Prosecution will go at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I did want to raise an objection in the way the question was phrased. It would appear that the Prosecutor is indicating that this was, in fact, a conversation. Had he, for instance, couched his question as it would appear at least from here that these two gentlemen, then at least it qualifies it. But without the qualification, it's as if Mr. Obrenovic is given an intercept which is supposed to be true, accurate, and complete. And that has not been established. So I don't object to Mr. McCloskey saying "I will hand you what -- an intercept, and it would appear that these two individuals are identified" and then at some point later on, when the intercept people come in, he can lay the proper foundation. But for Mr. McCloskey to say, "This is an intercept, and these two people, including Major Jokic, are conversing in this particular intercept," I think that is way beyond the foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understand your objection. Maybe, Mr. McCloskey, you could rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, all I was doing is identifying what is said on the document. I'm not trying to put a value judgement on it at this point. It merely says on the document: "9.10 hours between --" and it's a conversation between Zivanovic and Major Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if you let the witness answer the question, it will be much better rather than you give some indications on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm just trying to be clear for the record on what we're talking about. But I -- thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to review this intercept, Mr. Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. McCloskey. You supplied us with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does the information in it sound at all familiar to you, to what you were involved in on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I don't see -- Mr. McCloskey asked: "Does it sound at all familiar to you?" Does he mean do you recognise the circumstances of the situation? Evidently Mr. Obrenovic did not hear the intercept, so he couldn't recognise it as sounding like what he heard that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Maybe your question is too broad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll be here for a long time, Your Honour. But I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand. I understand. What if we take a break at this moment, and then we come back to these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at quarter to 11.00. Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I was just rising --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You are too eager to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, this intercept that is here, is that an intercept that has been provided to you for a long time by the Prosecution as part of the discovery materials?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, yes. Perhaps two years ago, thereabouts, I couldn't tell you the exact date. It is probably recorded somewhere, but yes, we did get that a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Looking at the third paragraph where it says -- where J allegedly says: "They were crushed on Vela Glava, and now there's a huge group moving towards the Drina. According to intelligence, towards Zljebac and Mladevac, the group is huge, absolutely enormous." Now, is that information that you were aware of at the time?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I was on the spot where that was happening, that is to say at Snagovo, and one of our platoons at Dzafin Kamen, commanded by Aco Kostic, did enter into combat with the column, and this is what we sent to the operations duty officer via the radio centre. We didn't say that the group had been routed but had been divided into two parts, and the rest of it is as we see here. We said at the time 45.000 men. So that for the most part reflects what was going on in the field at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, let's keep going down a little further. M asked: "Which intelligence officer?" And J says: "Dusko Vukotic." And who is Dusko Vukotic?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, Dusko Vukotic is a captain, assistant chief of staff for intelligence in the Zvornik Brigade. And at the point this was going on, he was located exactly at Kula Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And as this later on says: J says: "Yes, Kula Grad, to the left of Kula Grad." So that's where Dusko Vukotic was at the time and you know that by personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so. I ordered him on the 13th in the morning to go to Kula Grad and to organise or link up with the civilian police, and he was in fact at Kula Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then it says: "Mane needs to be informed immediately." And then it says in parentheses: "Mane, a MUP employee, most likely a chief." Again, tell us who you think Mane is?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, this refers to Lieutenant-Colonel Mane Djuric who was the deputy chief of the security centre in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then J asked: "Whom should I inform?" And M responds: "The Zvornik public security centre. They're there now. The army is doing other work at the moment." Do you have an opinion on what he means by "the army is doing other work at the moment"? And if you have to speculate, we don't need your speculations. If you have an opinion that you think is credible, we would like to hear it.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps General Zivanovic meant something with respect to the activities being under preparation for Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the VRS was preparing to attack -- well, was actually attacking Zepa on the morning of the 14th. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. On the next page of this intercept, J says at the top of the page: "The chief of staff, Obrenovic, is coming now, so we'll take steps immediately." Now, I take it the chief of staff, Obrenovic, is you. And what do you --

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What does this "is coming now, so we'll take steps," do you know what that means?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Jokic assumed that I would come to the Zvornik headquarters on the basis of some -- something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know what that basis was?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say. I can't say or define that. Probably on the basis of the fact that he had information that large forces were moving towards Zvornik, so he thought I should be in Zvornik. But that's just a guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So at 9.10 in the morning, after this -- after 9.10 in the morning, did you go back to the Zvornik Brigade headquarters on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to the next exhibit, P124/A. Just again, this is also an item that was provided in discovery a long time ago that you've had a chance to review before this. So if you could just take a brief look at it, I'll ask you a question or two. It says that it's 11.30 hours -- sorry, 20.38 hours, on the 14th. Again, this is allegedly a conversation between Zivanovic and Major Jokic. Do you see any of the information in this that appears to be incorrect or any indication that this has been falsified in any way?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to the form of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It assumes that the gentleman is capable of knowing the content within this intercept, and so I don't think there's a proper foundation made so he can give an opinion as to whether something was falsified or... So perhaps it could be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could respond to that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This witness, as the deputy commander of the Zvornik Brigade, has testified that he is very familiar with the way in which the Zvornik Brigade communicated. He has explained all that. He's also explained that he was aware that the enemy could capture their transmissions. He has also explained that he, as in the previous intercept, is living the events that are described in these various statements. And I believe it's perfectly fair to see if any of the facts in this document that he finds to be not true or problematic in some way that would give us an indication that these were not genuine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that your question is proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In this particular intercept, do you see any indication here that there is anything wrong or false or a mistake?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think that this conversation for the most part reflects the situation as it happened. Perhaps there might be some very minor mistakes as concepts, but not as what was actually happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next one. P125/A, this is from 14 July allegedly, an intercept at 21.02 hours. The document states that it's Palma duty officer Major Jokic and Badem. Can you remind us what Palma is.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, Palma was the code name in communications for the command of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Badem, what is Badem?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Badem was the same name for the commander of the 1st Light Brigade in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the first line says: "Hello Badem. Let me talk to Beara." You've already told us who Beara is. And then B says: "Who wants to talk to him?" And then it says: "The Palma duty officer wants to talk to him. Beara is needed urgently. Somebody needs him. The superior command urgently needs him, but he has to call me." So when it says the Palma duty officer wants to talk to him, at 21.02 hours, who was the Palma duty officer, the duty officer at the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 14th, Mr. McCloskey, it was Major Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then we go down a little further: "Hello, who is it, Major? I'm the duty officer at Palma. I need Beara urgently. This is Major Jokic. Who is that? Why the fuck are you not answering? Is Ostoja there?" Are there times when you were having problems making connections between the radio switchboard and other relays?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have an opinion as who Ostoja is in this context?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think that this was Ostoja Djuric who was a sort of logistics man for the rear, or something in the engineers company of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about Brko? "Is Brko there?" is the next line.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, Brko was the nickname of the deputy komandir of the ceta, company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what was this person's position? Brko?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brko was the deputy commander or komandir of the engineers company, and at the same time the assistant for morale, that that was what his post was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And the conversation goes back to: "Here is Beara. You have him on the line." And then J says: "Hello." And then X says: "Hello. Is the operations duty officer looking for me? Go ahead. Vojanovic is not here. He is up at Snagovo." Do you know who Vojanovic might be?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think there's an error here. I don't think it should read Vojanovic. It probably refers to Major Ljubo Bojanovic. Perhaps the person listening in didn't hear well. We didn't have a Vojanovic there as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that should be a B, as in Beara, not a V as in Victor?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, just in the last few lines that I mentioned, the subject goes from Beara who we know who he is, to some junior people at the engineering unit. And now it's talking about Bojanovic who is up at Snagovo. Can you help us at all in explaining how three subjects are all talked about within about eight to ten lines?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, as I understand what is written here in this document here, it's the following: Major Jokic, who was on duty, called the Bratunac switchboard and asked for Colonel Beara. While he was being connected, Jokic spoke on another phone with the engineers company at the same time, and the line to Bratunac remained open so that what he was talking about on the other phone with the engineers company could be heard on that line. And this is where he mentioned Brko and, as it says here, Vojanovic, but I think it's Bojanovic. In my view, he was speaking on two phones at the same time, and there were many such occasions when this happened. There was a lot of communication going on and all the lines were crowded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. As we go down in that conversation, it says: Is that Beara? Jokic here." And then: "BE: ..." And then J says: "We were together, Colonel. Sir, Number 155 called you and asked you to call him urgently." First of all, what was the rank of Beara at the time?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beara had the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what do you think "Number 155" referred to?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: 155 was the number of the extension on the main staff switchboard at Panorama.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think as you said before, can you remind us who you believe answered that extension?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Miletic, as I've already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then the -- it goes on to repeat, "number 155 that's, I mean, superior command. You go ahead and call them. You have to, so I don't speak like this." Then: "BE:..." Then J: "Yes. Hey. We have huge problems over here." BE is another... And then J says, "There are big problems. Well, with the people, I mean, the parcel." What do you think this sentence means?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the word "parcel" refers to prisoners. That's how it was used in this context in order not to speak openly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And -- all right. And then it says: "Who? Drago is nowhere around." And who do you believe Drago would be in this context?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Drago refers to Drago Nikolic who was a second-lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You mean chief of security of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then there's a remark at the bottom of the page that says: "Remark, thanks to the switchboard operator's mistake at Badem, we recorded a conversation between X and Y who couldn't be heard while he was intercepting and the line 44 was open for Jokic." Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this remark refers to what I explained just a short while ago, but in my understanding, it wasn't a mistake by the switchboard operator, but probably Mr. Jokic was speaking on two lines at the same time, both lines were open, so that simply the relay registered what he was speaking about on our internal connection with the engineers company. But evidently, the person who was listening realised that two conversations were being mixed up here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to P126/a. This is another intercept from 14 July allegedly at 22.27 hours, noting participants General Vilotic and Jokic, the duty officer from Palma. Are you aware of any general in the VRS named Vilotic?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. McCloskey. I think that again, probably because of the modulation or something else, the person who was listening didn't hear well. I think that this refers to General Miletic probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And it starts off: "Where is Obrenovic?" "He is in the field." Do you know where you were at 22.27 hours on 14 July?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do. I was at Snagovo near the crossroads at Borik [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As you read this over, does this information in this intercept comport with your knowledge of the events as they were happening at the time?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask some specific questions. It goes on to the second page, and J says: "Well, that's it. And those ones promised me some reinforcements, but they still haven't arrived, you know." And then V says: "From where?" And J says: "Well, the blue ones." Who do you think the blue ones refers to?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I assume that Mr. Jokic is referring to the civil police who wore blue uniforms. That's why he says "the blue ones."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then the intercept goes on to say: "Well, check that with Vasic," et cetera, et cetera. Who again in the context of this conversation would Vasic be, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, this is Colonel Dragomir Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then further on down the page, J says: "Obrenovic is really engaged to the maximum." Is that a true statement of your situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. McCloskey. At that time, we were still fighting at Snagovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then it goes on: "We are all, believe me. This packet has done the most to ruin us, and since this morning we have been reporting on the number of people, well, well so." And Vilotic says: "Okay, don't talk to me about that." "This packet has done most to ruin us, and since this morning we have been reporting on the number of people," what do you think he refers to when he says "packet"?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the word "packet" refers to war prisoners who had been brought in on buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And "reporting on the number of people," what are those people in your view?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, as I understand this, he says "since this morning, we have been reporting on the number of people," I think he's speaking of the column that wanted to break through, the column of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's go to the next one, P128/a. This is an intercept allegedly from 15 July, 9.39 in the morning. This is a brief intercept. Can you just tell us what you -- what they're talking about.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, this is an intercept that took place at 9.39 hours between duty officers Jokic and the duty officer at Zlatar. I understand that a report is being made to Major Jokic that our unit is returning from the Zepa region headed by Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic, and they are coming back to Zvornik. They're not saying this openly because they're probably aware that this is being intercepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then P127/a, again, 15 July allegedly, 10.00 a.m. in the morning. And we have participants Pandurevic, Jokic, Mijatovic. Can you tell me who you think these three are.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Mr. McCloskey. Jokic is Major Jokic; Mijatovic is Captain Miladin Mijatovic who was in the rear of the command of the Zvornik Brigade; and Pandurevic, Lieutenant-Colonel Vinko Pandurevic, who was our commander, the commander of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where do you think Pandurevic was at the time of this intercept, or at 1000 hours?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was in the command of the Drina Corps in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why is that? Why do you conclude that or how do you conclude that?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that on his way back from Zepa, he dropped into the command of the Drina Corps in order to get information as soon as possible about the situation in the Zvornik Brigade, and that he had this conversation while he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, if we could go to a document from the 15th of July. It's an interim combat report from the command of the Zvornik Brigade to the Drina Corps in the name of Vinko Pandurevic. And looking at the first page of this document, the first three paragraphs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, what's the number of that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. 139/a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Looking at the first three paragraphs, is it fair to say that that's a description of the military situation in the Zvornik Brigade area?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, looking at paragraph 4, it says: "An additional burden for us is the large number of prisoners distributed throughout the schools in the brigade area, as well as obligations of security and sanitary/technical measures in the field." And can you tell us in your view "the large number of prisoners," who does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think that this expression, "the large number of prisoners," refers to prisoners of war from Srebrenica who were brought from Bratunac to the Zvornik area and put into schools, as it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "As well as obligations of security..." What do you think that means?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think what it says here, "obligations of security," refers to guarding the prisoners of war who were in the schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are there --

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Guarding them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are there two ways of saying security in your language, as in guarding prisoners as security and the security branch of a unit?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this word "security," as it's in this paragraph, does it refer to the security branch in any way?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it refers to guarding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Go ahead. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I mean guarding the prisoners of war in the schools to prevent their escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what word is used to say "security" in B/C/S, in this context?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here "obezbjedzenje".

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If it means obligations of the security branch, what word would be used?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably it would say just this. It would say "o baveza organa bezbjednosti".

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in English it says: "Sanitary/technical measures in the field." In B/C/S, that makes a reference to asanacija. What is meant in this context by "asanacija" in your view?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Restoration of the terrain or sanitation means, to put it very simply, burying. Here it refers to burying people who had been shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. The next paragraph says: "This command cannot take care of these problems any longer as it has neither the material nor other resources." What problems do you think he is referring to in this sentence?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, he is referring to the danger caused by the arrival of the 28th Division into the defence areas of our three left-wing battalions and the difficult military situation so that now this had to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When he says: "If no one takes on this responsibility, I will be forced to let them go," who do you believe he's referring to when he says "let them go"?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's probably referring to the prisoners of war in the schools which are mentioned in the previous paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to Exhibit 129/C, a 16 July intercept at allegedly 21.16 hours, between Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic who asked to be connected with General Krstic at Zlatar, but was connected with the OC. Can you tell us what you believe the "OC" is in this context.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, OC is the operations centre of the Drina Corps command. This is the room in which the duty operations officer of the Drina Corps was with all his communications equipment, documents, his assistant, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And it starts off with: "Hello, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic speaking." And then it says: "Rasic here. Can I help you." Who do you think Rasic is?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, if I recall well, Major Rasic was the commanding officer in the security organ of the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did he have a nickname of Rale?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so from this context, but I can't remember his nickname from my own experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then Popovic says: "I was just up there." Knowing the situation as you do and having reviewed this intercept, what is your opinion on what Popovic is talking about here?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think that Popovic, when he says "I was just up there" means the forward command post of the Zvornik Brigade in Kitovnice. He's alluding to the fact that he was with the boss. I think that this refers to our boss, or rather Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And when Popovic a little down the page says: "Well, you got his interim report," what do you think that means?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this statement refers to the interim report of Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic of the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In part, did that report describe the very difficult situation that the Zvornik Brigade forces were in on the 16th where people were killed that you have described earlier?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's no references in that report regarding the prisoners or asanacija, is there?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then P says -- Popovic says: "It's all just like he wrote. I was there on the spot and saw for myself he had received some numbers." What do you think Popovic means by that?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he says "I was there on the spot," he probably means to say the place where the fighting was taking place at Baljkovice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I know I have a running objection to all these intercepts, but this is so full of speculation on the part of Mr. Obrenovic, it can't be ignored at this point. He's speculating on what Popovic means and where he's going, and I believe that Mr. McCloskey has crossed the line right now as to whether this person can testify accurately on any contents of these documents at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think from those intercepts, at least this witness could give us some information as far as he knows about the contents of these intercepts. And we quite understand that he's not a person personally involved in those conversations, and all his testimony is his opinion or speculation, if we may say it like this. We bear in mind about that. But let's not rule out the possibility for him to give us some informations about the contents of these intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to bring to the Trial Chamber's attention that before when the speculation was allowed, it was within the Zvornik Brigade. It had to do with the duty officer or it had to do with Pandurevic or it had to do with somebody present within the Zvornik Brigade that he maybe had some personal knowledge of, but it was still speculation. Here we have a main staff person named Popovic and General Krstic in a conversation that Mr. Obrenovic has no personal knowledge about. So this is another level above the speculation that he has already been speculating about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I did not distinguish the several levels of the speculations. Maybe Mr. Karnavas could shed some light on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, frankly, I don't have a particular problem with Mr. McCloskey's line of questioning; however, I did note that earlier he remarked to an interim combat report dated July 16. And I don't know whether he misspoke, whether it was July 15, the one we just talked about. But it hasn't been introduced, and I was just wondering, I wanted some clarification whether that was going to be introduced because there seemed to be some sort of a dialogue between Mr. Obrenovic and Mr. McCloskey. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I have the same doubts about that. How could the interim report be filed on the same day as the conversation. Maybe Mr. McCloskey could shed some light on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this intercept is being discussed at this time by this officer because it affects an issue related to the Bratunac Brigade, as was a major issue in the Krstic case, whether or not the Bratunac Brigade came up -- or members of the Bratunac Brigade came up and assisted in the executions at Branjevo military farm. The Prosecution has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think we'll see that on the next page of the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct. The Prosecution has some information it didn't have before that indicates the possibility that Mr. Popovic is not talking about prisoner burial operations only in this conversation.
