That's according to Mr. Obrenovic's viewpoint, and that's why I'm bringing out Mr. Obrenovic's viewpoint, so the Court can see his viewpoint on this issue which was important in the previous trial, to help clarify an issue which is important. My reference to the 16 July interim report was merely to emphasise that that report did not have to do with prisoner issues; it had to do with military issues. And so the reference in this intercept has to do with military issues, not prisoner issues. A report that has to do with military issues, not prisoner issues, which is supporting Mr. Obrenovic's viewpoint that he has gone to the front, he is meeting with Pandurevic. These are military issues. Whereas it was not clear in the previous trial whether this was military issues or prisoner issues. It is the viewpoint of this officer that at this point, he's talking about military issues. So to keep this record as fair as possible, I wanted this Court to see this. Mr. Karnavas and I have spoken briefly about this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. McCloskey is quite correct. On the second page, the entire conversation turns on the interpretation of "up there" which was a major issue in the Krstic case and which was also focussed upon by Richard Butler. And part of the problem, and I think this is perhaps why the Prosecution is raising this with Mr. Obrenovic, is apparently there is some linguistic differences, nuances in the way folks in Bosnia use the term versus folks in Belgrade, for instance. And I believe Mr. Obrenovic's interpretation is what we believe the interpretation to be, and I believe he's going to testify, that there are two different conversations ongoing at the same time. And as a result of that, based on the Butler report, the Trial Chamber in Krstic made some findings of facts which we believe to be erroneous. And in fact, I have all of the necessary paragraphs which I intend to point out to the Court after Mr. McCloskey covers this area. But we feel that Mr. McCloskey is correct in this instance in trying to clarify a very major point, and we -- in fact, we not only welcome this, but we commend him because we believe that this is part of his exculpatory duties. And so I want to raise that and I want to compliment as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I understand what you mean. But as for the issue, I believe the better chance for you to raise it is during your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree. But hopefully, if the Prosecutor does a nice job on direct, I won't have to clarify anything. And I think that's the route that he's going. But we'll see when we get to the cross, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey, we believe this matter as well as the testimony of Mr. Obrenovic is a related matter. You may proceed. Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're just still asking for the July 16th interim combat report if he's going to be referring to it with this witness, we would like to have him present it to us for consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have it at your hands?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't have it at my hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have some extra copies available?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sure Ms. Stewart can find it, Your Honour. It has been referred to in this intercept for many years now. But we can find it. That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We do have it, Your Honour. We could be of some assistance. I believe we marked it as D49/1. At least, that's what I'm told by Ms. Tomanovic, and if she says, it has to be pretty accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, but I believe that Ms. Sinatra is entitled to have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We can provide that, Your Honour, for Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. Yes, Ms. Sinatra. Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: If I could just glance at Mr. Karnavas's report, and then I'll hand it back to him if that would be all right with the Court, so I'm familiar with it as we're going along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me go back to that paragraph that says: "I was there on the spot and saw for myself he had received some numbers." What do you think that refers to "some numbers"?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think that the term "some numbers" refers to what Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic in his report speaks about the strength of the column of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And then it says: "Well, that's not even important... I'll come there tomorrow, so tell the general... I've finished the job." And then it says: "You finished?" And then Popovic says: "I finished everything." What do you think that refers to, the reference to "finishing the job"?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, this observation "I finished the job" spoken by Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic on the 16th, I believe refers to the solving in Pilica and Branjevo involving the execution of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's keep going down. And he says: "I'll come there tomorrow when I'm sure that's all been taken care of, you know." What do you think he means by that?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I'm come there tomorrow," that means that Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic would come to the command of the corps, the corps headquarters, where General Krstic was because he was looking for him. And when he says that "all been taken care of," I think it means the remainder of the burials. On the 16th, the people shot had still not been buried. I'm thinking of Pilica here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then it goes down and says, "After I bring a transport from there," and then Rasic says, "Right." And then Popovic says: "Well, in general, there weren't any major problems, but up there there were horrible problems. And that thing the commander sent, it was just the right thing." What do you think he means when he says: "Well, in general, there weren't any major problems..."? And if you know. You don't have to speculate. Just tell us what you make of this, if anything.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this refers to two things. In the first part is what he was doing around Pilica, and the second part is where he makes the observation that that's the thing that the commander had written and about the horrible problems. That's in Baljkovice and the horrible problems that emerged from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So just to be clear: "Well, in general, there weren't any major problems," what do you think that refers to?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that that refers to the part of the job around -- concerning the prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then when he says: "But up there," where do you think he means when he says: "But up there"? What location do you think he's talking about?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he's talking about the location at Baljkovice, which is where most of the fighting took place, the broader area around Baljkovice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And so -- and it says: "That thing the commander sent, it was just the right thing." What "thing" do you think he's talking about that the commander sent?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the interim combat report sent by the commander dated the 16th, referring to the fighting and the casualties and all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And when it says "the commander sent," which commander do you think he's talking about?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic, the commander of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then Popovic goes on and says: "Just the thing... Horrible... It was horrible." What do you think he's talking about then?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's talking about the fighting, where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then Rasic goes on on the next page and says: "Tell me, did anything arrive there now from Vidoje Blagojevic"? Popovic says: "From Vidoje?" Rasic says: "Today?" Popovic says: "Yes... You mean manpower?" Rasic says: "Yes, yes... Did anything arrive? Something was supposed to arrive." And then Popovic says: "Yes, it arrived. It's up there." What do you think he's talking about, Popovic now, when he says: "Yes, it arrived. It's up there"?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think he's talking about reinforcements which on the 16th when this conversation took place arrived from the Bratunac Brigade. And when I say "up there," I've already said that I think he's referring to Baljkovice and the locations where the heaviest fighting was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it goes on to say: "It's up there, but it didn't arrive on time. And it wasn't brought in on time." And then it says: "And the others who arrived, did arrive, but they were late, and so they weren't brought in on time and that's why the commander who was here had problems." What do you think that means?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think what it means is this: I said last week that I started asking for reinforcements on the 14th in the morning and on the 15th. We kept entreating them to send reinforcements, but they didn't arrive, and so we weren't able to stop the column of the 28th Division on time and it reached the front end of the battalion. And we suffered heavy losses and had to undergo heavy fighting, and this reflects the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then Rasic goes on to ask about what time Blagojevic's men arrived, and Popovic says he'll check. And if we could then go to the next exhibit, P130/a. This is an intercept allegedly from 16 July at 21.26 hours, just maybe ten minutes after the previous one. Participants Colonel Cerovic and the Palma duty officer. Can you remind us who Colonel Cerovic is.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, Colonel Cerovic was the assistant commander of the Drina Corps for moral guidance, morale, information, and religious affairs in the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And it says that Colonel Cerovic was informed that at 2100 hours, 30 men came from Badem (from Vidoje Blagojevic) and then at 1705, 30 men came from Dobos, and at 1725, a hundred men came from Banja Luka. Can you just tell us what those various places are.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, from Vidoje Blagojevic, this thing, it was about the Bratunac Brigade and the commander Colonel Blagojevic. 30 men arrived from Dobos, Dobos is the code name for the 1st Milici Light Infantry Brigade from Milici. 30 people also came from there, and from Banja Luka at 1725, 100 of them. That is from the company of the 1st Krajina Corps, in fact. And they arrived in the evening of the 16th. Let me also mention that on the 15th at around noon, another group of men numbering 50 to 60 men from the Bratunac Brigade arrived, and I talked to three of these men and their commanders when I interrupted the meeting with Vasic and Borovcanin in my own office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could go to the Exhibit P133/A, and if we --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a book, a logbook. And just -- I think it would be simpler if the witness could see the original logbook. We provided copies. But in order to keep it safe, we would prefer that it stay in the custody -- the original stay in the custody of the Prosecutor and that this witness be allowed to refer to the original logbook. It is a rather important document, and I think the Court may want to see the original as well. If we could put the English, on page 7, on the ELMO. And if the witness could be... We'll have the witness to see the original, if we could. Could the witness take a look at the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, first of all, could you tell us what this book is. What's it called and what is it?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, this is a working book of the duty officer for the 29th of May until the 27th of July, 1995. It was kept by the operations duty officers in the Zvornik Brigade, each for his shift. And they would record its working textbook. And they would note down anything they considered to be of any importance, and it's the book that I found in Mali Zvornik, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this exhibit is something that you provided, your Defence counsel provided us pursuant to your plea. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Before we get to this actual book, can you describe the other logbooks that a duty officer has to deal with so we can understand where this book fits in to this range of responsibilities? Can you just briefly outline this book and what other books they have. We do have some of those other books that may be relevant, but if you can just give us a rough outline of these various books and what they do and what responsibilities are.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the operations duty officer, at least in the Zvornik Brigade, kept two other similar books. One was the duty shift book, or logbook, and it had a set form and was kept for every shift. In addition to that, there was another logbook in which the handing over and takeover of duty was recorded. And the records would be made of the shift that had just taken place, and the commander would sign the shift takeover. And there was this workbook which was -- work notebook which was always at hand, and the duty officer, the operations duty officer, would write down straight away anything that he considered to be important. And he would use that book to fill in the logbook or diary on the basis of that book and to write out his report to the commander. He would use this as a reminder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Which one do you have in front of you now, P133?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the workbook of the duty officer, the operations duty officer. When I say "duty officer," I mean operations duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that's the book that is used in order to fill out the more normal logbook that you've also described?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to Mr. McCloskey testifying. If the evidence is going to come out what the logbook is used for, it needs to come out of the witness's mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, you may rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think you've made it clear. Let me ask: In the sequences of how books are used, can you explain where this book fits in to the sequence of how they're used.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, it comes first. So if I'm the operations duty officer, the telephone rings and somebody is reporting something to me, I take this workbook and record what the conversation was about if I consider it to be important. Then I use that, as I've already said, to introduce the vital information into the logbook or operations logbook. And then when I go on to write the -- write out the log or duty shift book, when shifts are handed over, then that's the way we do it. For keeping a workbook, there were no regulations to say how you were supposed to keep it. Each duty officer would decide for himself what he was going to write down in his workbook.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So this you call the workbook. The next one is the logbook. Do we have the logbook, the next one in order that you referred to? Is that one that you provided the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the blue book with the blue covers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to that. And then you've described another book that showed the shift -- a shift-change book. Did you provide that to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. McCloskey. I didn't come by that document because I didn't find it together with the other documents. I didn't have it, so I didn't hand it over either, provide it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this particular book, the workbook, in -- after the war, did you ever show this workbook to Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I did not show this workbook to Mr. Jokic, but I did show several pieces of paper copied out from this workbook, what he wrote down in his own hand and the things that referred to the 14th of July when he was the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you identify from the original book that you have in front of you which pages of it you showed to Dragan Jokic? And --

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- You're familiar with the ERN number system, so if you could just tell us the page of the ERN number that you recall showing to Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think I showed a copy and the last three numbers are 745.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And for the --

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next would be 746.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And just for the record, 745 is page 8 of the English translation. 746 is page 9 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's page 10 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's page 11 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Page 12 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Page 13 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Page 14 of the English.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: And 752.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Page 15 of the English.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure now whether I showed page 753 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in -- did you ever study this particular document and add anything to it after the war in preparation of your Defence?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. I looked through this workbook, and on some pages, the duty officers hadn't written the date clearly. It wasn't precise. In some places, the date had been entered; and in others, it hadn't. So I tried to work out where a new day began.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Not where a new day began, the interpreter corrects herself, but the place from which that duty officer started writing in the book, that is, when his shift started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I wanted to determine or attempt to determine what was written by which duty officer in order to make sure. At first, I didn't know exactly when what duty officer was on duty, but I tried to clarify the whole picture in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you had had the duty officer change of command logbook, would that book have helped you determine which person was a duty officer at which time?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Then I would just have to read what it said there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. That's not a book you had; it's not a book you got from Mali Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I didn't get that book. I didn't find it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if we could -- I want to go through some of these entries with you, and if we could start with your ERN number 7 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, it's time for a break. If you've finished the foundation of this document, we'll break here, and then you'll come to the contents after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And we're pretty close to the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. And we'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, those pages of the workbook that you showed -- you said you showed to Mr. Jokic, when you -- when roughly in time did you show those to him?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I showed copies of these pages to Major Jokic a little before our arrival to have an interview with you in Banja Luka in April 2000, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was your purpose of showing him those pages?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I wanted to see whether he wrote those pages and whether he remembered that. And secondly, I wanted to get him to tell the truth about me, and that's, I think, what I said to him. I said to him that he should tell the truth about me, and as for the rest, he could say whatever he wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did he say, if anything, when you showed him those pages?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked him whether he had written that. I said: "Is this your handwriting?" That's what I said, or something like that. And he said: "Yes, where did you get this?" Then I said that's my own business, and then we read it together. We were sitting at right angles at a table.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how many of those pages did you read together with Mr. Jokic at that time?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we skimmed through what it said without going into analyses. And those were the pages that I have just said I probably showed him, those few pages, what I said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did he indicate that any of those pages were not his handwriting?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go in your book to the page before the one that you believed you showed to Mr. Jokic. That is, the ERN ending in 744. And if you could take a look at that. And is there anything on that page that you have actually added yourself in this -- in the review that you did that you described earlier?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, on page 744, just before the last paragraph, I wrote in pencil: "1407" and then I wrote the name "Jokic" in the Latin alphabet, and underlined it with three lines. And I did all this in pencil.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In the English, that's page 7 of the translation. Can we put the original on the ELMO just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. Obrenovic, if you can point to the ELMO where you actually -- if we could bring it up a little higher, perhaps. Can you point on the ELMO where the markings were that you did.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, just before the last paragraph on the right-hand side of the page, this is what it says: "14th of July, Jokic." I wrote this in. This here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So how did you know it was 14 July and Jokic? On what do you base this conclusion from this pencilled note?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, to put it briefly, there are three things I have to say: First, Major Jokic and I worked together for a long time so we could recognise each other's handwriting. Secondly, as I said, I asked Dragan Jevtic whether he knew Jokic's handwriting. And he confirmed this. And thirdly, I went in chronological order looking at the sequence of events. And you will see the notes on the previous page and the times entered in, and on the basis of this I assumed that this was it. I said this was not 0000 hours on the 14th, but in my view the beginning of the shift, the first note made during that shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So this handwriting that we see next to your 14.07 Jokic, in the English, it says: "Colonel Salapura called - Drago and Beara are to report to Golic." Do you recognise this handwriting that says that?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I am no graphologist, but it seems to me that this is Jokic's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You stated that the next page in the book was where you first began showing Jokic pages of the book. Do you recall whether or not you showed him this one, the 744, or did you actually, like you said, start at 745, regarding the ones you actually showed Mr. Jokic?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure I showed him page 745. As for page 744, I'm not sure. I may have shown it to him, but maybe I didn't. As far as I can remember, I copied those pages that contain exclusively his handwriting, not somebody else's. So I can't be certain about page 744. I can't be more precise than I have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. In your review of this book for the time period of the 13th, 14th, 15th of July, did you recognise events noted in this book that you had actually had participated in personally or knew about personally?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we'll go over some of those. But let's first start with -- take a look with 744 at the bottom of the page where you've written your 14.07 Jokic. And it's written in handwriting in the original. "Colonel Salapura called." Who is Colonel Salapura?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Salapura, I can't recall his first name right now, but it will come back to me later, but he was the commanding officer of the main staff who was in charge of the intelligence service of the main staff, the intelligence administration, of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petar was his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Drago. Who do you think "Drago" is in this first sentence?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Drago refers to Second-Lieutenant Drago Nikolic who was in charge of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you've discussed Beara already. How about Golic? Who do you think Golic is?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think Golic refers to Major Pajo or Pavo Golic, probably Pavle, I'm not sure. But they called him Pajo, and it refers to him. And he was one of the -- of the men in the intelligence service in the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right, let's go now to your 746, which is page 9 of the English. And it starts out and says: "1000 hours, Palma 1, situation in battalions is regular." We've heard about Palma. Is Palma 1 different? If so, what is that?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I think it says here Palma II, and I think it refers to the forward command post of the Zvornik Brigade which was at Dzajica Brdo in the village of Kitovnice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction. And in the next line, "1024 hours, Osmaci - informed Lieutenant Djuricic about the movement of Muslims." What's that?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, Mr. McCloskey, Osmaci refers to the village of Osmaci, and also the Osmaci Tactical Group from the 1st Birac Brigade which was our left-hand neighbour. And Jokic probably informed Lieutenant Djuricic who was the command of the Osmaci Tactical Group about the movement of Muslims. Last week, I said that after the morning fighting the column divided, and one part set off in the direction of the Drina, and the other part in the opposite direction in the village of Osmaci. And he is informing our left-hand neighbour, which is the usual procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that would be the Muslim column, then, that's a reference to?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then the next line is: "1500 hours, Colonel Beara is coming." Did you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that point in time. On the 14th, after noon, I found out from Major Zoran Jovanovic that Colonel Beara had brought a large number of prisoners in on buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then it says: "Colonel Beara is coming." And then: "In order to," and then it says, "Orovoc, Petkovci, Rocevic, Pilica." What do you think Orovoc refers to?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Orahovac, and that there is an error here in the entry. That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about the other three places: Petkovci, Rocevic, Pilica?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the three villages where prisoners of war were kept in the schools, and I spoke about this last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go in your book to 750, page 13 on the English translation. The first line says: "Pelemis's TG" and then in slashes written by our translation unit, it says "tactical group." And then it says "has problems with manpower." What do you think this is a reference to?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, in my view, this means -- TG could mean telegram from Pelemis saying that he has problems with manpower. He was the deputy of the commander in Pilica and he is probably saying that he has too few men to guard the prisoners and that the people from the village of Pilica were upset because the prisoners had been brought there. That's how I interpret this. It could mean tactical group, as you said, but I think that my interpretation is the correct one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is there another Pelemis that this may refer to?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're right. There is also Lieutenant Miso Pelemis who was the commander of the 10th Sabotage Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that was the -- Drazen Erdemovic's group that participated in the executions at Branjevo farm on 16 July?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For technical purpose, I'm going to object to that. It's leading. He hasn't established this. I know it's hypertechnical, but it's an improper way of getting through the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey, maybe you could put your question another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Mr. President. I did not think that was any matter of dispute, is why I abbreviated it. But I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did Miso Pelemis have a unit that was to your knowledge involved in any of the events in the Zvornik Brigade area?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what unit would that have been?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the 10th Sabotage Detachment of the main staff. And according to my information, they were in Petkovci and in Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to page 13 of the English and page -- sorry, page 14 -- page 14 of the English and page 751 of what -- of your original. Let's start with the first sentence from Premijer, "Turks captured our men." Do you have any idea what that is a reference to?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. Premijer refers to our intercept group of the Zvornik Brigade that was deployed at Gucevo. And according to me, Premijer told the duty officer that listening in to enemy conversations, they had got information that as it says here, "Turks captured our men". I think this refers to Captain Zoran Jankovic who was really taken prisoner on the 14th in the evening after the fighting at Snagovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And Premijer, again, what is that for again, just to remind us? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a code name referring in communications to our group listening in to enemy radio conversations. They listened to the enemy radio communications for the needs of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. How about this next line: "Jokic, delegation from Pilica"? What do you make of that?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I learned later, that evening a delegation arrived from Pilica in order to protest because the prisoners had been brought to Pilica, to the centre of a village. I think that's what this means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then do you know why -- well, again, do you recognise the handwriting of this statement, "Jokic, delegation from Pilica"?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is Jokic's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know why Jokic would write his own name down in the book?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then we come down a few more lines and it says: "Beara has to call 155." Whose handwriting does that look like to you?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Same as your last answer?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what do you think this is a reference to, Beara has to call 155?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, if I may draw a comparison with the intercepts we had before where this was discussed, 155 is the extension of the switchboard at Panorama, the main staff. And Beara was to call that extension.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next page. It's your 752; it's page 15 of the English. Again, this handwriting at the top of the page "from Beara," do you recognise that handwriting?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's the same as in my previous answer. I think it is Major Jokic's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And "Drago to report" and then "Mane Dukici," "0900, Beara is coming." Is that the same handwriting in your view?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This last part that's written out, there's several lines, seven lines, and it's entitled: "Report for the corps." And it starts out: "Tonight at around 2020 hours, in the wider area of Maricici, a large group has passed" and it describes the situation. I won't read it all. And it ends by, "Find a possibility to send more forces for intervention in the morning." What is this?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, this is the handwritten report that refers to the interim report I held here in my hand perhaps an hour ago, which on the 14th, between 23 and 24 hours, I wrote down on a piece of paper and gave to my communications man to send to the duty officer. And he sent it on to the operations duty officer. And probably this is what he noted down and later sent on to the corps command. And I wrote this for Snagovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go another exhibit. It's P134. If we could get the original book. 134/A. And the English translation, page 6 on the ELMO, please. Could you take a look at that exhibit, that book, and tell us what book that is of the various books you have been describing to us.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, this is the duty-shift book of the barracks duty officer. So this is not the operative that's on duty, but one step below him. This is the duty officer of the barracks in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is --

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- That person's position, what the duty officer of the barracks does and what this book is.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the duties of the barracks duty officer pertained to internal duty. That means that he looked after the cleanliness of the barracks, that he made sure that the guards were there on time. He took care of the raising and lowering of the flag and the mealtimes and the units, the lining up of the units to go to the restaurant for meals. He took care of the traffic within the barracks compound, the security and safety of the traffic there. So that his duties were limited to internal order within the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And could you go to the page that deals with July 9 and 10, 1995, which is the first page of the English transcript that we have. Down at the bottom -- well, first of all, we see a report on the situation in the barracks, and then a couple of paragraphs that provides a brief description of the situation. Then we see down at the bottom: "Duty relinquished by, certified by, duty assumed by." Can you tell us what the purpose is of those three headings?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, on the left-hand side of this page, it says: "Duty relinquished by," that is, the person who was the duty officer up until then, the previous day, and finished off with the 9th in the morning. And "Duty assumed by" is the new person taking over the shift. And in the middle, it says: "Certified by." The signature is illegible. It could have been certified by myself, the operations duty officer in the headquarters, or somebody like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you make out the signature of "duty relinquished by" on your original?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't make out the signature, but from the heading I see it is Sergeant First-Class Goran Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: So judging by that, that would have been him, although I don't remember the signature and it's not legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is there a signature under certified by?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is. It's just initialled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next page, then, the 10th and the 11th. And is there a signature under the certified block for these dates?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is. I signed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. What time did you sign it, if you recall, or...? If you don't, what time would it be normal for you to sign something like this?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps the latter part of your question is the better one. It's difficult for me to say exactly what time, but the usual time was sometime in the morning, between 8.00 and 9.00. 8.00 and 9.00 a.m. At a time it was 8.00 a.m., later on it became 8.30. And then 9.00. So the most precise answer would be in the early hours of the morning, between 8.00 and 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page for the 11th and 12th July. Who signs the certified block down there, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is the signature of Sreten Milosevic probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that on 11/12 July?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. For the 12th and 13th, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about 11/12?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: 11/12, I was the signatory there. That's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next one 12/13. Who is that again?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the 12 and 13th, I think that this was the signature of Captain Sreten Milosevic, assistant for the rear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next page, 13/14. This is page 5 of the English transcript. Is there a signature there on the original?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is. I think it's Major Dragan Jokic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next page, page 6 of the English, which is 14/15. Is there a signature under the -- well, it says in English "Control," the one between the relinquished by and the duty assumed by.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that's completely blank on the original?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, in the situation, it notes that among other things: "A bus with prisoners stayed overnight at the compound of the barracks."

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who would that have been?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably a bus of prisoners from Bratunac, driven in from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the 15th and 16th. Is there a signature between the duty relinquished by and the duty assumed by, the control as we have seen it before, or the certification from the other pages?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a signature in the left-hand corner who relinquished duty and none in the "duty assumed by," or the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And just the last one, page 16 or 17, can you make out any signature of the certified on that particular day? Does anyone certify the changeover of duty?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 16th through the 17th of July, 1995, somebody did initial the document certifying it, but I can't recognise who that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to P137/A. Again, we'll hand you the original book. Just for me to make clear, the last book we were talking about, P130 -- sorry. 134, was that a book that you provided in this group of material pursuant to your plea?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And -- okay, so getting to what you referred to as the blue book, P137/A, can you tell us what that book is.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, this is the logbook of the operations duty officer in the brigade command. And I said a moment ago that this was one of the books kept by the duty officer in the Zvornik Brigade, and it was compiled according to regulations by the JNA. The format is provided for in the rules and regulations. So in recording information in this logbook, you had to adhere to the principles prescribed. And that's where this logbook differs from the other books where we just had notes jotted down inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If we could put the English translation on the ELMO, if you could just briefly take a look at the 11 -- it goes 11, 12, 15, 17 July, and then 18 July in the English, are there any dates missing in that original book?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. We have the 9th, we have the 10th and 11th, the 12th. And then we jump to the 15th. So what is missing on this page is the 13th and 14th. We have a blank sheet, and then we don't have the 16th, but we continue with the 17th. And once again, we're missing the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, can you tell by your examination of that original book whether or not there was anything ever written in for those missing dates? For example, is there any indication that there was anything ripped out of that book?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing was ripped out of the book. Everything is as it was originally. And then in lead pencil we see at the end some additions made on the last few pages, but just an identification of the individuals, and I did that myself. Other than that, nothing has been added to or tampered with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you offer an explanation why those dates are left out.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this happened for two reasons. The first reason is this: I've already explained that actually. Major Jokic, after my arrival on the 15th in the morning at HQ, told me that Colonel Popovic had ordered that nothing should be entered concerning the prisoners and all that business. And the second, realistically speaking, in the brigade headquarters, there was quite a lot of chaos. The situation was chaotic, if I can put it that way. So I assume they just didn't find the time to keep the administration up to scratch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So the information that's noted on the dates that are in this book, there's no reference to prisoners or locations of execution sites or anything like that, is there?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're quite right, no mention of that is made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If we could go to Exhibit P131/a. This is a document from the general staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, 14 September, 1995, under the signature or the name of General Ratko Mladic. It says: "Urgent, attention, command of the Drina Corps, logistics sector of the general staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, copy to the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade for their information. "This is to approve 5 tonnes of D-2 diesel fuel for carrying out engineering works in the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps. The logistics sector of the general staff of the Army of Republika Srpska shall deliver the fuel to the Standard barracks in Zvornik, to Captain Milorad Trpic. Captain Trpic shall be responsible for the accurate maintenance of records on the number of engine work hours of engineering machines, and account accordingly for consumption of fuel." Is there a Captain Milorad Trpic in the Zvornik Brigade or was there at that time?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, there was no Captain Trpic. And I think this is a printing error, a typing error. And I'm sure that this refers to Captain Milorad Trbic, with a B and not a P.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. What do you believe this fuel was for at the time?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, this fuel was needed and later used for tanking up the mechanisation for the engineers and the trucks that performed the reburial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Whose decision was it to open a corridor for the Muslim column, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. McCloskey, this was a decision made by Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were there any consequences from superior command as a result of him making that decision to let those Muslims go that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I can say - I don't know whether consequences is the right word to use - but that already on the 16th in the afternoon, as far as I know now, and I learned immediately after the event then, they ordered Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic to come and -- or rather, Colonel Popovic to establish where Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic, what the conditions of the agreement were. That is to say, a sort of investigation was conducted. And later on, I think on the 18th, a group of officers came from the main staff. And in addition to other business, they looked into that affair, too. They were two colonels, these commanding officers. I saw it as being them checking out why Vinko had done that, done what he did. And that from the main staff -- that the main staff and the superior command didn't look kindly towards his conduct and actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, there is less than 10 minutes left. Mr. Karnavas, are you going to do your cross now, or we have our break and continue at 3.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would say let's continue at 3.00, if that's okay with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll resume at 3.00 this afternoon. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.19 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I thought that we could begin by just going over your background a little bit and before we jump into the various subject matters. As I understand it from listening to your testimony, you began your military career at the age of 15 basically by attending a military secondary school. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then after that, you went on to the military academy at the age of 18, and you graduated, I believe, when you were age 23.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you put that quite correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if my information is correct, as I understand it, you were at the top of your class, if not the number one student in your class. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean, judging by my marks or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Judging by your marks. As I understand it, you were an excellent student; outstanding, in fact. That was the term that I was told.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I graduated from the military gymnasium with excellent results, and the academy, I completed as the first among armoured units, and I was fifth in the other courses. The overall result, I came fifth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as you just indicated, just recently and then in your direct, you specialised in the armoured and mechanised units. Is that correct? Your training at the academy, the military academy?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That is what I specialised in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And can I assume that someone with your basic training or education, that you were headed for a career as a combat commander, as opposed to, say, in the engineering unit, just to pick an example?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try and be precise in responding to your question. So in precise terms, I completed the ground forces academy and the armoured units, the land army, that is. And as far as your question is concerned, in the former JNA, there was several combat services such as the infantry, armoured and mechanised units, the artillery, and the engineers unit that you mentioned was not a combat unit, a combat service. It was only after the war that it became a combat service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So, as I understand it, you graduated in 1986.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you understood it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And by April 1993, at a fairly young age, you had achieved the position of chief of staff of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that that's a fairly -- you rose pretty high up to that position?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could put it that way. There were no commanding officers, so I suppose that was the result of that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That in part was because of the war, lack of officers, but also I think it would be fair to say that you were also an excellent soldier.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was my superiors who made that assessment. Perhaps they bore in mind all that. But I think the main reason was that there weren't sufficient qualified commanding officers to go around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now in 1992, the Zvornik Brigade was formed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd of June, 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when it was initially formed, would it be fair to say that it was a fairly disorganised and dysfunctional brigade, initially as it was getting formulated?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I share your opinion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But by 1995, the Zvornik Brigade had become fairly disciplined and fairly large in size in comparison to other brigades, such as, for instance, the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, the Zvornik Brigade was an infantry Zvornik Brigade, establishment-wise, and a large number of units and men and the machinery it had and the equipment it had it had from the light infantry brigade which was far smaller. Now, as to the second part of your question with respect to the quality and organisation of the unit and whether it was disciplined or not, the Zvornik Brigade was a well-disciplined unit, generally speaking. If you look at the other units of the Drina Corps and the Army of Republika Srpska, no worse, no better than the others. It was a sort of standard-type unit. And I would say that it was far from the desired level of military organisation. If you take NATO as your parameter or a similar organisation, then it would lag far behind. But one knew who did what in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I think you could say the same if you were to make the comparison between the JNA and the VRS, that there was some differences as far as the quality in those two?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The VRS was of lesser quality than the army units of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You relied more heavily on reserve officers as opposed to professional officers such as yourself?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the -- would it be fair to say also the soldiers in the VRS were more -- more like citizen soldiers, that is, that they were reservists as well, serving two weeks or what have you at a time as soldiers, and then going back to their homes or their farms. And so there was this constant rotation where they were on duty for a couple of weeks, and then off duty for a couple of weeks. Would that be fair to say? I know I'm generalising right now.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, generally speaking, that would be a fair assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, are these set of questions relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it does become relevant throughout the trial. Maybe not particularly to the Prosecution's case in chief, but at some point it does become highly relevant, especially when the Prosecution introduces Mr. Butler, their military expert who believes or at least is of the opinion that the VRS is of equal calibre as the JNA. So here we have a military expert, graduated first in his class. Certainly he's highly qualified to give us an insider's point of view. He's also a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would hope we could avoid characterisations of Mr. Butler's opinions because I think that is a mischaracterisation. And from what Mr. Karnavas has just said, it appears he is going well beyond the scope of the direct examination in his cross, which if he chooses to call this witness in his own case, that's fine. I have not objected thus far. I'm not -- but I hope that he will stick to the parameters of the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: In the cross-examination, I believe that the Defence counsel could ask whatever questions they like, but the condition is those questions should be relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So that's why I asked you about the relevance of your questions. But maybe, you know, for those questions, I hope you get over as soon as possible and come to the most crucial matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we were to compare the Zvornik Brigade with the Bratunac Brigade, would it be fair to say that at least in numberwise of resources and soldiers, or battalions, the Zvornik Brigade was twice as large as the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I really don't know in exact terms what the number of men was for the Bratunac Brigade. I know that it had four battalions, infantry ones, and I knew that it had less men than the Zvornik Brigade. Now, the ratio, I really can't talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, the Zvornik Brigade had eight battalions, one of which was donated, in essence, to the Bratunac Brigade. Is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think we can say that. The Zvornik Brigade, if we're talking about that period of time, July 1995, had seven infantry battalions. And before, dating back to 1994, our 8th Battalion by decision or rather by order of the Drina Corps commander was resubordinated to the Bratunac Brigade. And in the command sense, that was the 4th Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade. So you can't speak about donations of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you look at it in that sense, you're correct. However, was not the Zvornik Brigade in some sense financing or supporting, providing resources for the 4th Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade, formerly known as the 8th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The rear of the Zvornik Brigade secured what we called salaries and some personal remuneration of that 4th Battalion, or what was the 8th, whichever you'd like to call it, as well as the rear, butt, the quartermaster section, that is to say, the uniforms and food part of the logistics. The ammunition and combat equipment was under the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So the 4th Battalion, and I believe it was Radika Petrovic who was in command of that battalion, was subordinated to the Bratunac Brigade during this critical period that we're discussing here today? Or of this trial. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. The term used was resubordinated. These are important military terms, so I'm going to object to the mischaracterisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I didn't see that word, resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It can't be resubordinated. It has to be subordinated because it belongs to the Zvornik, and then now it's subordinate to the Bratunac Brigade. But perhaps the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes. Well, Mr. Karnavas, you may put your question in another form so as to clarify whether it's resubordinated or subordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, was the 4th Battalion, formerly the 8th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade, was that subordinated to the Bratunac Brigade or resubordinated? Help us out here.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, to avoid any misunderstanding, it was completely under the command of the Bratunac Brigade during that period of time, just as its 1st, 2nd, or any other unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I think that solves that. Now, on -- the reason I asked the question was because on July 12th, I believe, one of your officers, Dusko Vukotic, I believe, who was your intelligence officer, was sent, was he not, to the 4th Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade with respect to the captured prisoner?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was sent to the area of the 4th Battalion. Not only with respect to the prisoner, but to arrive at the relevant information and intelligence that the neighbouring unit possessed and which would be of use to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But just so I'm clear, Mr. Vukotic was not asked to contact the intelligence officer of the Bratunac Brigade, Momir Nikolic; rather, he was asked or directed to go directly to the 4th Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade. Am I correct on that?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And one of the reasons for asking him to go there was you wanted some information from this particular prisoner as far as where the 28th Division was, where were they headed, the numbers, and so on and so forth. You were looking for intelligence information you might be able to get from this particular prisoner. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But not only from the prisoner, but generally speaking from the spot, from the area, both from the prisoner and all other available information there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, while we're on the subject, if I could ask you to clarify a point, and I would like you to look at a part of an interview statement given by Mr. Vukotic on September 17th, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And for the record, it's D47 for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps you could help us out here. In English, it would be page 53. And I'm looking at lines 14 all the way through page 54, line 5. I apologise for not locating the B/C/S portion for you. But if I could assist you and perhaps you can locate the area. There's a conversation where you're -- where he's being asked about Radika Petrovic, and to whom he has to report. And he seems to be indicating that he reports both to the Zvornik Brigade, and also to the Bratunac Brigade at the same time.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I can't find that portion. What line did you say it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Line 14, but it was in English, 53, page 53.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the B/C/S version here in front of me. So line 14 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It might be somewhere around page 47, 48, 49, somewhere around there. I believe it begins at the bottom of the page 48, on line 23 or so. And if you go to page 49, at least it seems to me from looking at the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, does it not say here, at least that it is his opinion, Mr. Vukotic's opinion, that Radika Petrovic, the commander of the 4th Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade, was reporting both to you as commander of the Zvornik Brigade, and to Colonel Blagojevic, commander of the Bratunac Brigade? Does he not seem to be saying that?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here, but may I be allowed to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that that particular battalion was subordinated to the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, and that is absolutely correct. Now, I think in the summer of 1994, on behalf of the commander, Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic, I was personally in the command of the Bratunac Brigade, the headquarters there, and the brigade commander at the time was Lieutenant-Colonel or Colonel Slavko Ognjenovic. And I handed the battalion over to him, and the order was at the time, the corps commander had in fact ordered that that battalion should come under the command of the Bratunac Brigade and that their communication, their links were adjusted accordingly, that they should become part of the composition of the Bratunac Brigade. And that's how it stood until this 4th or 8th Battalion appeared in Zvornik on the 20th of July in the morning, 1995 that year was. I might have made a slight mistake on the dates. But what Vukotic says is quite normal, and according to the rules, the neighbouring brigade, and I spoke about this three or four days, would be reporting, or rather informing their neighbours. They would be informing their neighbours. So not only did we receive relevant combat intelligence from the Bratunac Brigade, which was our right-hand neighbour or our neighbour in the rear, but we also received information and intelligence from the 1st Birac Brigade which was to our left. So this same man, Vukotic, on the 12th was at Osmaci, with Lieutenant-Colonel Djuricic with the same assignments, to gather information and intelligence which could affect the combat situation where we were. So that's what all is about. When it -- we can't say that he's reporting. The regular standard army procedure was that the subordinate informs his superior. And this is an exchange of intelligence amongst neighbours. Our right neighbour called us up to inform us about one thing or another. So that's what Vukotic is in this context here, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Would part of that process also be, for instance, the intelligence officer, the chief of intelligence for the Bratunac Brigade, would he not also be passing on information directly to Mr. Vukotic? Would that also be part of the process?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometimes yes, sometimes no. It was customary to inform the superior first, your superiors first, and then your neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to go a little bit into Krivaja 1995 and discuss the various orders on that. But before I get there, perhaps we can look at the map and discuss that a little bit. And I believe it has been marked as P138 for identification purposes. I wanted to ask you a couple of questions. As I understand it, prior to and even during and after the fall of Srebrenica, there were some permanent division lines between the RS territory and the BiH territory where you had the 2nd Corps facing, at least in your area, the Zvornik Brigade. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. From the right, or rather the northerly border of the zone, the area, right up to the Spreca River.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not on the map, but this area here. Perhaps a little further off, up until the village of Osmaci, was the brigade zone. And units of the 2nd Corps, or rather some of its divisions, the 4th or 5th. I'm not quite sure which.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The record should reflect that the witness pointed at the Exhibit P138 for identification, and was able to show us with his light, red light, where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And those lines had been pretty much fixed for some time prior to July 1995, had they not?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a general way, yes. There were some changes in the area of the 5th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade, then in the 2nd Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade as well, in this area, in the months of April and May 1995. But as for the rest, all the other lines had been fixed in 1992, or more specifically in 1993, and not changed since with the exception of those two that we had mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So on one side, you would have the 2nd Corps of the Muslim army, more or less at that borderline, and on the other side the VRS would have its troops, specifically where you were pointing out, primarily it was the Zvornik Brigade who was responsible for that area which was part of the Drina Corps. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And so when the 28th Division was leaving the Srebrenica area, they were actually in RS territory, were they not, trying to -- crossing RS territory. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of course, they were trying to get to their side, which meant they would have to break through the RS line -- VRS line, which on the other side had the Muslim 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. You have -- after the fall of Srebrenica, the 28th Division is on the offensive, are they not? They're the ones that are on the move, so militarily they're considered to be the offensive -- on the offensive. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that they were trying to break through from an area in which they were surrounded. It's part of a combat operation, a break through from an area in which they were surrounded. That's how they referred to it themselves in their own documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- and as I've indicated, not only by breaking through the VRS lines, you, as part of the VRS, would also be facing the 2nd Corps from the opposite side as well, and that could cause or pose some problems, would it not?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. More significantly in terms of the strength and equipment, the 2nd Corps forces were much stronger, and they posed much more of a danger for the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could -- as I understand your testimony, sometime towards the end of June, June 29th I think the date was, Lieutenant-Colonel - was he Colonel? I don't know. I think he was Lieutenant-Colonel - Pandurevic came to your residence and asked you to come back while you were convalescing from an injury?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 29th in the evening. That's when he came, that's what I said, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, as I understand it, your commander played a rather significant role on the offensive in the takeover of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Unlike, for instance, yourself, you were left behind with the Zvornik Brigade to, more or less, maintain the positions that you already had and which were fixed for quite some time?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I then received an order from the commander that if I took all the necessary measures -- that I should take all the necessary measures to protect ourselves from the 2nd Corps. The assumption was that the units of the 2nd Corps would try to give some relief to the units of the 28th Division, and that they would attack us, that's what we expected. And those were my orders, the orders that I then received from my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. So if I could show you several orders, and maybe we can discuss them. And I'll begin by showing you what has been marked as D16/1 for identification purpose. And it's the July 2nd Drina Corps order. If you could first just look at it and see if you recognise it and if you've ever seen it. Have you seen this order before, Mr. Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I've seen it before. This is an order for active combat activities operation number 1, from the command of the Drina Corps dated 2nd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it you saw it back then in 1995. Is that a fair assumption? Did you ever come across this back in 1995, or was it just recently through your lawyers that you had an opportunity to actually see the order itself?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be very accurate on this. At that time, I knew that I would not join the attack on Srebrenica, and I didn't pay much attention to these combat orders, orders directly relating to combat activities concerning Srebrenica. I may have seen it at that time. I can't be sure, however. I did see it when my lawyers showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander laid this document out, and it was clear enough at the time. I didn't mind that then particularly at that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If you could focus on paragraph number 5, and it's on page 3. If you could just look at that quickly. It's called "Tasks." I believe under that paragraph, you should find a specific, designated task for the Zvornik Brigade. Do you see it, Mr. Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Obrenovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, Mr. Karnavas. I've read it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
